solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Small cloth covering uncooked black fruit (10)

indicatorNotes.covering: the cloth is wrapped over the other pieces, so they sit inside it

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
terry is the looped cotton towels are made of

annotation.surface: Something dark and uncooked lies under a little cloth, like a covered dish on a kitchen table.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Black fruit' reads as one item, blackberry perhaps, but black belongs to the wordplay and the fruit is red.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain case of definition by example: the strawberry is one of the commonest soft fruits.

entries.clue: Call about training to return for field event (4,3)

indicatorNotes.about: the call goes around the training
indicatorNotes.to return: the training comes back the other way, PT to TP

annotation.surface: A coach calls about returning to training ahead of an athletics meet.
annotation.walkthrough: Training as physical training is a British school convention worth learning; the surface makes it sound like athletes' practice.
annotation.definitionFit: The shot put is an athletics field event, throwing a heavy ball.

entries.clue: Fish counter about to stock mud pie (3,6)

indicatorNotes.about: the counter turns round, TELLER to RELLET
indicatorNotes.to stock: the counter holds the mixed-up mud inside, as a shop stocks goods
indicatorNotes.pie: pie (or pi) is printers' jumbled type, so mud pie is mud in a jumble

blocks.note: a teller counts money at a bank

annotation.surface: A fishmonger's counter is about to stock a mud pie, a strange item for the display.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fish counter' reads as a fishmonger's slab, but fish is the definition and the counter is a bank teller. Pie as a mess of type is an old printing word.
annotation.definitionFit: The red mullet is a small reddish sea fish.

entries.clue: Changing platforms and not spending a penny? (6,8)

annotation.definition: Changing platforms and not spending a penny?

blocks.note: the surface wants railway platforms; the setter means computer operating systems, and moving between them
the plain sense: looking round the shops without buying anything

annotation.surface: Someone moves from one station platform to another without paying a penny.
annotation.walkthrough: Split it differently: WINDOWS HOPPING, jumping between computer platforms. Browsing shops without buying is the plain sense. 'Spending a penny' is also British slang for using a toilet.
annotation.definitionFit: Window shopping is looking at goods in shops without buying anything.

entries.clue: Associate of Hull Science Museum’s inside (3)

indicatorNotes.inside: the answer lies within the words Science Museum

annotation.surface: A partner of a Hull museum works inside London's Science Museum.
annotation.walkthrough: Hull is not the city: Rod Hull was a British TV entertainer whose act was an unruly Emu puppet on his arm.
annotation.definitionFit: Emu was the puppet that shared Rod Hull's act, so it was his constant associate.

entries.clue: Share offer a reason for demonstration? (6,5)

blocks.note: new shares offered to existing shareholders
an issue of rights, such as civil rights, that people march over

annotation.surface: A market announcement and a protest placard appear side by side.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, jokey reading: civil rights are an issue people march about.
annotation.definitionFit: A rights issue is an offer of new shares to a company's existing shareholders.

entries.clue: Perhaps flat fish can be caught with it (4)

annotation.definition2: fish can be caught with it

blocks.note: British slang for a home, of which a flat is one kind

blocks.clueFragment: fish can be caught with it
blocks.note: an angler's hooked pole for landing big fish

annotation.surface: A flatfish might be caught with some tool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flat fish' reads as plaice or sole; split them. Gaff is British slang for your home, a flat perhaps.
annotation.definitionFit: A gaff is someone's home, and also a hooked pole for landing big fish.

entries.clue: Stomach tender in casualty? (5)

blocks.note: to tender is to offer, a bid
A&E, accident and emergency, is the British hospital casualty department

annotation.surface: A patient with a tender stomach is waiting in the emergency room.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is medical: tender stomach, casualty. But stomach is a verb, to put up with, and tender is an offer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: if you cannot stomach a person, you cannot bear them.

entries.clue: I’m left injured outside small shooting range (7)

indicatorNotes.injured: the letters are hurt out of shape
indicatorNotes.outside: the jumbled letters go around small

annotation.surface: Someone left injured outside a small shooting range, a gun club accident.
annotation.walkthrough: A shooting range is a gun club in the surface; here shooting means filming.
annotation.definitionFit: A film set is where a movie is shot.

entries.clue: Patient profile in the post? (3,11)

blocks.note: the surface wants a hospital patient's file; the setter means a portrait of the Bible's most patient man
not the mail: a post is a position of employment, and the profile sets out its duties

annotation.surface: A hospital patient's medical profile arrives by mail.
annotation.walkthrough: Job in the Bible is the model of patience, so a profile of Job is a Job description. A post is also a job, and the description sets it out.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, it is the document profiling a post; read as a pun, it profiles the patient man of the Bible.

entries.clue: US sculptor’s work rejected, silly blunder in it (9)

indicatorNotes.rejected: the work is sent back, GO to OG
indicatorNotes.in it: the scrambled word goes inside the work

blocks.note: a go is a turn of work, as in 'give it a go'

annotation.surface: An American sculptor's work is turned down because of a silly mistake in it.
annotation.walkthrough: Claes Oldenburg made giant sculptures of everyday things like clothes pegs and ice creams.
annotation.definitionFit: Claes Oldenburg was a Swedish-born American pop-art sculptor.

entries.clue: A little iron piece placed around window (5)

indicatorNotes.piece: a piece of the words is taken

annotation.surface: A small iron fitting is set around a window frame.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the letters backwards across 'little iron'.
annotation.definitionFit: An oriel is a bay window jutting out from an upper floor.

entries.clue: Record turned out badly — Holst didn’t know it (5)

indicatorNotes.turned: the record is flipped round, LP to PL
indicatorNotes.badly: the letters of out are put together wrongly

annotation.surface: A recording of Holst came out badly, and the composer never knew the piece.
annotation.walkthrough: Holst's suite The Planets was written before Pluto was found in 1930, so it has no Pluto movement.
annotation.definitionFit: Pluto was discovered after Holst wrote The Planets, so it is the planet he did not know.

entries.clue: Whiff of decay in iron I removed from order (9)

indicatorNotes.removed from: the I is taken out of the word for order

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

annotation.surface: A smell of rot is traced to some iron, and someone wants it cleared out.
annotation.walkthrough: Order here is tidiness, not a command.
annotation.definitionFit: Fetidness is a foul smell, the whiff of something rotting.

entries.clue: Low support ahead of police pay (4,3,4)

blocks.note: the foot is the lowest support of the body
the Bill (Old Bill) is British slang for the police

annotation.surface: Police pay is so low it barely supports officers.
annotation.walkthrough: The Bill, or the Old Bill, is British slang for the police, and was a long-running TV police drama.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: whoever foots the bill pays it, the verb 'foot' once meaning to add up an account's total at its foot.

entries.clue: Viewer of arms business shot in the legs — it’s bad (10,5)

indicatorNotes.in: business and shot go inside the scrambled letters
indicatorNotes.bad: the letters of the legs it's are mixed badly

blocks.note: a pic is a photo, a shot

annotation.surface: An arms dealer has been shot in the legs, and it looks bad.
annotation.walkthrough: The arms-business-shot story is a gangland scene; the pieces are a company and a photo.
annotation.definitionFit: A telescopic sight is the magnifying scope mounted on a gun for aiming.

entries.clue: Became ill getting over hospital experience (2,7)

indicatorNotes.getting over: became is placed over hospital, holding it

annotation.surface: Someone who fell ill is recovering after a hospital stay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Became ill' reads as one phrase, and it is: the hospital letter splits it in two.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to go through hardship is to experience or undergo it.

entries.clue: What occurs that I will come out of unharmed? (7,1,7)

indicatorNotes.will come out of: the answer emerges from these letters rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone asks what must happen for them to walk away unhurt.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a plain question, so it is easy to miss that its first four words are the letters of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Escaping without a scratch means escaping unharmed.

entries.clue: House snake, tailless kind (7)

indicatorNotes.tailless: the last letter of the word for kind is cut off

blocks.note: a road or river winds, snakes

annotation.surface: A house snake, a harmless kind without a tail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'House snake' reads as a pet; snake is a verb here, and House is the royal family.
annotation.definitionFit: Windsor is the name of the British royal house.

entries.clue: Stink over tap routine (7)

blocks.note: hum = a bad smell in British slang

annotation.surface: A stink rises from the tap, the usual trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: Hum is British slang for a bad smell. In a down clue 'over' puts the first piece above the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as adjectives: a routine, humdrum job is one with nothing to break the monotony.

entries.clue: Possibly stole kiss with hunk (9)

blocks.note: a hunk is a big piece

annotation.surface: Someone may have stolen a kiss from a handsome hunk.
annotation.walkthrough: Stole looks like the verb; it is the fur wrap worn round the shoulders.
annotation.definitionFit: A stole is one kind of neckpiece, hence 'possibly'.

entries.clue: Caught, leading to wrong appeal (5)

blocks.note: to wrong someone is to harm them

annotation.surface: A batsman is given out caught after a mistaken appeal.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket, where fielders appeal to the umpire; here appeal is the noun meaning attractiveness.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a person's charm is the quality that draws others to them, their appeal.

entries.clue: Turned up with skirt for Jewish festival (5)

indicatorNotes.Turned: up is turned round, UP to PU

blocks.note: a skirt is an edge, a rim

annotation.surface: Someone turned up in a skirt for a festival.
annotation.walkthrough: Skirt is the verb or noun for an edge, not clothing.
annotation.definitionFit: Purim is a Jewish festival celebrating Esther's saving of the Jews in Persia.

entries.clue: Drive across a country (5)

indicatorNotes.across: the drive stretches across the A, holding it

blocks.note: a spin is a short drive in a car

annotation.surface: A road trip across a whole country.
annotation.walkthrough: A spin is a short pleasure drive.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Spain is one country of many, the broadest kind of crossword definition.

entries.clue: One fascinating plotter (9)

blocks.note: one who intrigues, schemes in secret

annotation.surface: A captivating schemer.
annotation.walkthrough: To intrigue is both to fascinate and to plot, so one word covers both.
annotation.definitionFit: An intriguer is one who intrigues: fascinates, or plots.

entries.clue: Go off around peak (3)

indicatorNotes.around: to come around is to turn about and face the other way, so the letters run backwards

annotation.surface: A climber sets off around a mountain peak.
annotation.walkthrough: Go off means spoil, as food does, not depart.
annotation.definitionFit: A tor is a rocky hilltop, especially on Dartmoor.

entries.clue: One inclined to drive before parking (4)

blocks.note: to ram is to drive hard, as a post into the ground

annotation.surface: Someone likes to drive around before finding a parking space.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inclined to' reads as tending to; the definition is something sloped.
annotation.definitionFit: A ramp is a sloping surface, one set on an incline.

entries.clue: Northern town’s odd Latin 19 (10)

indicatorNotes.odd: the letters are put in a strange order

annotation.surface: A northern English town has an odd Latin charm.
annotation.walkthrough: 19 points at the answer to 19 down, CHARM. Altrincham is a town near Manchester.
annotation.definitionFit: Altrincham is a town in Greater Manchester, in the north of England.
